claim: S-FLU is a pseudotyped replication-deficient influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/34 (PR8) virus that replicates only in cell lines expressing HA.
source: We developed previously a pseudotyped replication-deficient influenza A/Puerto Rico/8/34 (PR8) virus, which replicates only in the cell line expressing HA that provides the HA protein on pseudotyped virus particles for their binding to cells (Powell et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Powell et al., 2012, which describes the development of this virus system.

claim: The HA expressed by the cell line used to produce S-FLU can be derived from any virus subtype.
source: importantly, the HA expressed by the cell line can be derived from any virus subtype.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the S-FLU system, allowing for pseudotyping with different HA subtypes.

claim: NY-ESO-1 is a cancer testis antigen whose expression is normally restricted to germ cells but is highly dysregulated in some malignant cells.
source: NY-ESO-1 is a well-known cancer testis antigen (CTA). Its expression is normally restricted in germ cells, but it is highly dysregulated in some malignant cells (Thomas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thomas et al., 2018, which describes the expression pattern of NY-ESO-1.

claim: NY-ESO-1 may be therapeutically targeted without substantial risk of immune-related off-targeted effects due to the immune-privileged nature of germline cells.
source: Given the immune-privileged nature of germline cells, NY-ESO-1 may be therapeutically targeted without substantial risk of immune-related off-targeted effects.
evidence: This claim is based on the established knowledge that germline cells are immune-privileged and inference about the safety implications for targeting NY-ESO-1.

claim: Intranasal or intramuscular immunization with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response.
source: We found that intranasal or intramuscular immunization with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1B.

claim: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus immunization suppresses NY-ESO-1-expressing tumour development and spontaneous metastasis.
source: We found that intranasal or intramuscular immunization with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response and suppresses the NY-ESO-1-expressing tumour development and spontaneous metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from tumour models presented in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Co-administration of NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus with anti-PD1 antibody displays enhanced tumour reduction.
source: Moreover, with anti-PD1 antibody co-administration, NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus immunization displays an enhanced tumour reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: In vitro infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus results in expression of both influenza virus NP and NY-ESO-1 proteins in infected HEK 293T cells.
source: in vitro infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus shows that the influenza virus NP and NY-ESO-1 proteins were both expressed in infected HEK 293T cells, with a preferential localization within the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Influenza virus NP protein localizes preferentially to the nucleus in NY-ESO-1 S-FLU infected cells.
source: in vitro infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus shows that the influenza virus NP and NY-ESO-1 proteins were both expressed in infected HEK 293T cells, with a preferential localization within the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: NY-ESO-1 protein localizes preferentially to the cytoplasm in NY-ESO-1 S-FLU infected cells.
source: in vitro infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus shows that the influenza virus NP and NY-ESO-1 proteins were both expressed in infected HEK 293T cells, with a preferential localization within the nucleus and the cytoplasm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BALB/c mice infected via nasal route with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus displayed a higher level of infection on day 2 in lungs.
source: BALB/c mice infected via nasal route with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus displayed a higher level of infection on day 2 in lungs with higher frequency of infected EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells compared to immune cells (identified as CD45+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus preferentially infects EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells compared to CD45+ immune cells.
source: BALB/c mice infected via nasal route with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus displayed a higher level of infection on day 2 in lungs with higher frequency of infected EpCAM+ lung epithelial cells compared to immune cells (identified as CD45+) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus induces effective T cell proliferation of 1G4 cells in draining lymph nodes.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 clearly shows an effective T cell proliferation of 1G4 cells only in the groups of mice infected with the NY-ESO-1 S-FLU, which indicates antigen-specific priming at dLN.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTrace Violet proliferation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection indicates antigen-specific priming at draining lymph nodes.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 clearly shows an effective T cell proliferation of 1G4 cells only in the groups of mice infected with the NY-ESO-1 S-FLU, which indicates antigen-specific priming at dLN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the T cell proliferation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in HHD and BALB/c mice.
source: Figure 1B shows that intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in HHD and BALB/c mice
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing IFNγ-secreting CD8+ T cells in Figure 1B.

claim: The NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response induced by NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus is of lesser magnitude than CTL responses against immunodominant Flu epitopes for M1 and NP proteins.
source: Figure 1B shows that intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus elicits a robust NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in HHD and BALB/c mice albeit to a lesser magnitude than the CTL responses against the immunodominant Flu epitopes for M1 and NP proteins, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative flow cytometry data in Figure 1B.

claim: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus induces NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in spleen.
source: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus also induces NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus displays a specific cytotoxic effect in in vivo killing assay.
source: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus also induces NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) and displays a specific cytotoxic effect in in vivo killing assay (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo cytotoxicity assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A single infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU was sufficient to give significant protection against tumour challenge in a prophylactic tumour model.
source: Interestingly, a single infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU was sufficient to give significant protection against tumour challenge (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour nodule enumeration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Immunization with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus significantly reduced the number of nodules in lungs in a prophylactic tumour model.
source: In prophylactic tumour model, immunization with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus significantly reduced the number of nodules in lungs.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour nodule enumeration data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the therapeutic model, a higher number of tumour nodules developed than in the prophylactic model (~30–40% more).
source: In the therapeutic model, a higher number of tumour nodules developed than in the prophylactic model (~30–40% more)
evidence: This is a comparison of tumour burden between different experimental models based on data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Two sequential infections with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus significantly reduced the number of tumour nodules in lungs in a therapeutic model.
source: In the therapeutic model, a higher number of tumour nodules developed than in the prophylactic model (~30–40% more) and two sequential infections with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus significantly reduced the number of tumour nodules in lungs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour nodule enumeration data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Primary tumour displayed spontaneous metastasis to lungs at humane end point in the spontaneous tumour metastasis model.
source: In the spontaneous tumour metastasis model, primary tumour displayed spontaneous metastasis to lungs at humane end point
evidence: This describes the experimental observation in the spontaneous metastasis model shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mice that received two sequential infections with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus showed fewer colonies (p<0.05) than any of the other treatments in the spontaneous tumour metastasis model.
source: mice that received two sequential infections with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus showed fewer colonies (p<0.05) than any of the other treatments (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 2C with statistical significance.

claim: Intranasal infection did not elicit a high CTL response in spleen.
source: Despite inducing a strong CD8+ T cell response in lungs, intranasal infection did not elicit a high CTL response in spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing lung and spleen responses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Intranasal infection failed to protect mice from subcutaneous tumour challenge with NY-ESO-1-expressing 4T1 cells.
source: Furthermore, it failed to protect mice from subcutaneous tumour challenge with NY-ESO-1-expressing 4T1 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth curve data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A strong systemic immune response coordinated across tissues is required for tumour eradication.
source: A strong systemic immune response coordinated across tissues is required for tumour eradication (Spitzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spitzer et al., 2017.

claim: Intramuscular immunization with recombinant adenoviral-vectored vaccine has shown generation of CTL responses in multiple mucosal sites.
source: Previously, intramuscular immunization (i.m.) with recombinant adenoviral-vectored vaccine has shown generation of CTL responses in multiple mucosal sites (Kaufman et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kaufman et al., 2008.

claim: Intramuscular infection induced stronger NP and NY-ESO-1-specific CTL responses than intranasal infection in blood and spleen.
source: In the blood and spleen, intramuscular infection induced stronger NP (p<0.01) and NY-ESO-1 (p<0.01)-specific CTL responses than intranasal infection (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claim: Intranasal infection induced a significantly higher NP and NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cell response compared with intramuscular injection in lungs.
source: In lungs, intranasal infection induced a significantly higher NP (p<0.01) and NY-ESO-1 (p<0.05)-specific CD8+ T cell response compared with intramuscular injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 3B with statistical significance.

claim: An increased frequency of Flu M1- or NY-ESO-1 specific polyfunctional CD8+ T cells was observed in HHD mice spleen following intramuscular infection.
source: Similarly, an increased frequency of Flu M1- or NY-ESO-1 specific IFNγ (single producer), or IFNγ and TNFα (double producer) or IFNγ, TNFα, and IL2-producing CD8+ T cells (triple producers) was observed in HHD mice spleen following intramuscular infection (Figure 3C)
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A higher frequency of flu M1- or NY-ESO-1-specific IFNγ or IFNγ and TNFα-producing CD8+ T cells was detected in HHD mice lungs following intranasal infection.
source: conversely a higher frequency of flu M1- or NY-ESO-1-specific IFNγ or IFNγ and TNFα-producing CD8+ T cells was detected in HHD mice lungs following intranasal infection (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular cytokine staining data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Intranasal infection and intramuscular infection resulted in the accumulation of higher number of total Flu M1-/NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in lungs and spleen, respectively.
source: Moreover, intranasal infection and intramuscular infection resulted in the accumulation of higher number of total Flu M1-/NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in lungs and spleen, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by absolute cell number data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reciprocal distribution of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in lungs and spleen post intranasal infection indicates that effector T cells are mostly retained in lungs following intranasal infection.
source: The reciprocal distribution of antigen-specific CD8+ T cells in lungs and spleen in post intranasal infection indicates that the effector T cells are mostly retained in lungs following intranasal infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the distribution data, representing an inference from the observed patterns.

claim: Activated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells have been known to persist following recovery from respiratory virus infection.
source: Activated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells have been known to persist following recovery from respiratory virus infection and very late antigen 1 (VLA-1; α1β1 integrin) has been implicated in the retention of T cells (Hogan et al., 2001; Jennrich et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hogan et al., 2001; Jennrich et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2004.

claim: VLA-1 (α1β1 integrin) has been implicated in the retention of T cells.
source: Activated antigen-specific CD8+ T cells have been known to persist following recovery from respiratory virus infection and very late antigen 1 (VLA-1; α1β1 integrin) has been implicated in the retention of T cells (Hogan et al., 2001; Jennrich et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hogan et al., 2001; Jennrich et al., 2012; Ray et al., 2004.

claim: The expressions of VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, and CD44 were significantly upregulated on NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in the lungs of intranasally infected mice.
source: The expressions of VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, and CD44 (p<0.0001) were significantly upregulated on NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in the lungs of intranasally infected mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing tissue retention marker expression in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A with statistical significance.

claim: The frequencies of tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells (TRM) were significantly higher in intranasally infected mice.
source: Furthermore, the frequencies of tissue-resident memory CD8+ T cells (TRM) (p<0.0001) were also significantly higher in intranasally infected mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing TRM frequencies in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B with statistical significance.

claim: NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus can be pseudotyped with any HA in the envelope.
source: NY-ESO-1 S- FLU virus can be pseudotyped with any HA in the envelope
evidence: This describes a key feature of the S-FLU system design.

claim: Coating with relatively novel HA, against which antibodies are scarcely presented in the population, could nullify the pre-existing antibody mediated effect.
source: coating with relatively novel HA, against which antibodies are scarcely presented in the population, could nullify the pre-existing antibody mediated effect.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about how pseudotyping could overcome pre-existing immunity.

claim: NY-ESO-1- and NP-specific CTL responses were reduced in lungs following the infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus with matched HA/NA.
source: NY-ESO-1- and NP-specific CTL responses were reduced in lungs following the infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus with matched HA/NA (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing matched vs. mismatched HA/NA in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus with different HA coating (NY-ESO-1 S-FLU [PR8]) elicited stronger NP-specific CTL response in spleen.
source: Similarly in spleen, infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus with different HA coating (NY-ESO-1 S-FLU [PR8]) elicited stronger NP-specific CTL response (p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with statistical significance.

claim: NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in spleen was reduced in both matched or mismatched HA/NA NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infections.
source: However, NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response in spleen was reduced in both matched or mismatched HA/NA NY-ESO-1 S- FLU virus infections (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice treated with intramuscular injection showed a greater reduction in tumour size which was concomitant with significantly higher infiltration of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in TIL.
source: Mice treated with intramuscular injection showed a greater reduction in tumour size (p<0.05 on days 18, 20, and 24) and (p<0.01 on days 26 and 28), which was concomitant with significantly higher infiltration of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in TIL (p<0.01) (Figure 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A with statistical significance.

claim: Mice infected via the intranasal route did not show any difference in tumour size.
source: whereas mice infected via the intranasal route did not show any difference in tumour size (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: A higher number of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells still accumulated in lungs in intranasally infected mice.
source: We also investigated the distribution of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in lungs and spleen, and strikingly a higher number of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells still accumulated in lungs in intranasally infected mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was no difference in the distribution of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in spleen of intranasally or intramuscularly infected mice.
source: However, there was no difference in the distribution of NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in spleen of intranasally or intramuscularly infected mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The number of colonies in lungs following intranasal or intramuscular infection was not significantly different from each other but lower than the mice with no infection in clonogenic assay.
source: In clonogenic assay, the number of colonies in lungs following intranasal or intramuscular infection was not significantly different from each other but lower than the mice with no infection (p<0.001) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance.

claim: Reduced metastases to spleen were only observed in intramuscularly infected mice.
source: However, reduced metastases to spleen were only observed in intramuscularly infected mice as depicted in Figure 5C.
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Infections with recombinant NY-ESO-1 S-FLU and Hu-Ad5-NY-ESO-1 viruses display comparable CTL responses in lungs and spleen.
source: Infections with recombinant NY-ESO-1 S-FLU and Hu-Ad5-NY-ESO-1 viruses display comparable CTL responses in lungs and spleen
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fowl Pox infection did not elicit a stronger NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response.
source: whereas Fowl Pox infection did not elicit a stronger NY-ESO-1-specific CTL response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice treated with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection displayed a reduced tumour growth compared to the mice treated with Hu Ad5-NY-ESO-1 or Fowl Pox-NY-ESO-1 viruses.
source: Mice treated with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection displayed a reduced tumour growth (716.9 ± 125.8 mm3) compared to the mice treated with Hu Ad5-NY-ESO-1 (972.0 ± 90.6 mm3) or Fowl Pox-NY-ESO-1 (1137.4 ± 223.6 mm3) viruses (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour volume measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mice that received NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus demonstrated a lower number of 4T1-NY-ESO-1 clones derived from metastatic niches in lungs or spleen in clonogenic assay compared to the mice treated with Hu Ad5 NY-ESO-1 or Fowl Pox virus infection.
source: Moreover, mice that received NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus demonstrated a lower number of 4T1-NY-ESO-1 clones derived from metastatic niches in lungs or spleen in clonogenic assay compared to the mice treated with Hu Ad5 NY-ESO-1 or Fowl Pox virus infection (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Mice treated with intramuscular injection of NY-ESO1 S-FLU showed a greater protection against tumour challenge by displaying reduced tumour size compared to intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus or intramuscular injection with GFP-S-FLU virus or the mice with no infection.
source: Mice treated with intramuscular injection of NY-ESO1 S-FLU showed a greater protection against tumour challenge by displaying reduced tumour size compared to intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus or intramuscular injection with GFP-S-FLU virus or the mice with no infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cytotoxic T cells infiltrated to the tumour displayed a higher expression level of PD1.
source: We observed that cytotoxic T cells infiltrated to the tumour displayed a higher expression level of PD1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 4T1-NY-ESO-1 tumours positively responded to both anti-PD1 monotherapy and combined therapy with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection by displaying a slower tumour progression compared to isotype antibody treatment.
source: In general, 4T1-NY-ESO-1 tumours positively responded to both anti-PD1 monotherapy and combined therapy with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection by displaying a slower tumour progression compared to isotype antibody treatment (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The most pronounced tumour regression was observed in combined treatment with anti-PD1 antibody and intramuscular injection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus.
source: The most pronounced tumour regression was observed in combined treatment with anti-PD1 antibody and intramuscular injection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus (Figure 7B, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumour growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The anti-PD1 antibody administration did not increase the infiltration of the NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells into the tumour in NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus-infected mice.
source: The anti-PD1 antibody administration did not increase the infiltration of the NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells into the tumour in NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus-infected mice (Figure 7B, right)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anti-PD1 antibody administration was associated with increased expression of CD103 on NY-ESO-1-specific CTLs in TIL.
source: but it was associated with increased expression of CD103 on NY-ESO-1-specific CTLs in TIL (Figure 7B, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Anti-PD1 antibody monotherapy showed a reduced tumour metastasis to lungs in clonogenic assay.
source: In clonogenic assay, anti-PD1 antibody monotherapy showed a reduced tumour metastasis to lungs
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: In combined therapy with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection, anti-PD1 antibody demonstrated a significantly higher reduction in tumour metastasis.
source: and notably; in combined therapy with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection, it demonstrated a significantly higher reduction in tumour metastasis (Figure 7C) (p<0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by clonogenic assay data shown in Figure 7C with statistical significance.

claim: Live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is one of the strongest inducers of CD8+ T cell response.
source: Among many types of influenza vaccines, live-attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV) is one of the strongest inducers of CD8+ T cell response (Korenkov et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Korenkov et al., 2018.

claim: The S-FLU virus used in this study is similar to LAIV in terms of generating T cell mucosal immunity in mice and ferrets.
source: and the S-FLU virus used in this study is similar to LAIV in terms of generating T cell mucosal immunity in mice and ferrets (Powell et al., 2012; Nogales et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Powell et al., 2012 and Nogales et al., 2016.

claim: Intranasal immunization of NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus induced a robust specific CTL response in lungs but with a modest systemic CTL response in spleen.
source: Intranasal immunization of NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus induced a robust specific CTL response in lungs but with a modest systemic CTL response in spleen.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: The route of vaccine administration influences the intensity of the systemic antigen-specific T cell response.
source: The route of vaccine administration influences the intensity of the systemic antigen-specific T cell response.
evidence: This is a general principle supported by the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: H5N1 whole-inactivated virus (WIV) immunization via intranasal and intramuscular route induced a comparable frequency of multifunctional Th1 CD4+ cells.
source: H5N1 whole-inactivated virus (WIV) immunization via intranasal and intramuscular route induced a comparable frequency of multifunctional Th1 CD4+ cells (Trondsen et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trondsen et al., 2015.

claim: PR8 WIV strain infection induced a higher IFNγ-secreting CD4+ T cells in spleen only in intranasal route.
source: whereas PR8 WIV strain infection induced a higher IFNγ-secreting CD4+ T cells in spleen (Bhide et al., 2019) only in intranasal route.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bhide et al., 2019.

claim: A significantly higher NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in blood and spleen with intramuscular immunization is in line with a previous study.
source: We observed a significantly higher NY-ESO-1-specific CD8+ T cells in blood and spleen with intramuscular immunization, which is in line with a previous study (Budimir et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Budimir et al., 2013.

claim: An orthotopic 4T1 mouse breast cancer model used in this study resembles triple-negative breast tumours (ER-, PR-, HER2-) in humans.
source: An orthotopic 4T1 mouse breast cancer model used in this study resembles triple-negative breast tumours (ER-, PR-, HER2-) in humans (Luo et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Luo et al., 2020.

claim: 4T1 tumour cells used in this study express a lower level of NY-ESO-1, which may be comparable to the physiological level of NY-ESO-1 expression in human cancer.
source: and we have used 4T1 tumour cells that express a lower level of NY-ESO-1, which may be comparable to the physiological level of NY-ESO-1 expression in human cancer.
evidence: This is a characterization of the experimental model with speculation about its relevance to human cancer.

claim: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus protected the mice from lung metastasis induced by tail vein or subcutaneous injection.
source: Intranasal infection with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus protected the mice from lung metastasis induced by tail vein or subcutaneous injection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: S-FLU without NY-ESO-1 showed a partial but significant protection against tumour development in lungs.
source: Interestingly, S-FLU without NY-ESO-1 showed a partial but significant protection against tumour development in lungs (Figure 2A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Non-specific innate immune response mediated through TLR7 by virus single-strand RNA may be utilized for anti-tumour response.
source: suggesting that non-specific innate immune response mediated through TLR7 by virus single-strand RNA may be utilized for anti-tumour response (Chi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism supported by a citation to Chi et al., 2017.

claim: Full reduction of spontaneous metastasis was only achieved with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection, but without any impact on subcutaneous tumour development.
source: Nonetheless, full reduction of spontaneous metastasis was only achieved with NY-ESO-1 S-FLU virus infection, but without any impact on subcutaneous tumour development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Regional tumour protection with intranasal infection may be attributed to the continued presence of antigen-specific CTLs in lungs, which was associated with poor infiltration of CTLs into tumour.
source: Regional tumour protection with intranasal infection may be attributed to the continued presence of antigen-specific CTLs in lungs, which was associated with poor infiltration of CTLs into tumour.
evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the experimental data.

claim: Intranasal infection with influenza virus accelerated melanoma growth in skin with increased shunting of anti-tumour CD8+ T cells from the tumour site (skin) to distant site (lungs), resulting in decreased immunity within the tumour.
source: Recently, it has been shown that intranasal infection with influenza virus accelerated melanoma growth in skin with increased shunting of anti-tumour CD8+ T cells from the tumour site (skin) to distant site (lungs), resulting in decreased immunity within the tumour (Newman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2020.

claim: Increased upregulation of tissue retention molecules VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, and CD44 on lung CD8+ T cells following intranasal infection probably prevents the T cell migration to distal subcutaneous tumour site, thus permitting the uninhibited tumour growth.
source: Moreover, increased upregulation of tissue retention molecules VLA-1, CXCR6, CD103, and CD44 on lung CD8+ T cells following intranasal infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) probably prevents the T cell migration to distal subcutaneous tumour site, thus permitting the uninhibited tumour growth.
